stops.name: Alexandropol (Gyumri), the Greek quarter
stops.campa: In the Greek quarter of Alexandropol, on the frozen rim where three empires grind together, a son is born to Ioannis Giorgiades, a Greek carpenter, cattle-owner, and ashokh, and his Armenian wife Evdokia. The night itself is disputed: the family keeps New Year's Eve, the passport will one day say another year entirely, and the fog around the date is the first of his mysteries. The house smells of wood shavings and wool; Turkish, Armenian, Greek and Russian are spoken across a single supper table.

stops.name: Alexandropol, the grandmother's deathbed
stops.campa: His grandmother, past a hundred years old, calls the boy to her deathbed, lays her hand on his head, and binds him with her last strength: in life, never do as others do, either do nothing, only go to school, or do what nobody else does. The command enters him like a seed. At the forty-day grave rite he scandalizes the mourners by hopping around the grave and singing a rhyme of his own making; the injunction is already at work.
stops.quote: In life never do as others do... Either do nothing — just go to school — or do something nobody else does.
stops.quote_source: The grandmother's injunction as Gurdjieff records it, Beelzebub's Tales to His Grandson, 'The Arousing of Thought'

stops.name: Alexandropol, the Yezidi boy in the circle
stops.campa: In a side street the boy comes upon children tormenting a small Yezidi: they have drawn a circle around him in the dust and he cannot get out. He strains against nothing at all, weeping, as against a wall. Gurdjieff rubs away part of the line and the child shoots out like a bolt. The grown men he questions shrug or lie. He tests it later and finds it true: dragged bodily from the circle, a Yezidi falls into catalepsy. No priest, no schoolmaster, no book of physics will ever explain it to him, and the wound of not-knowing stays open for life.
stops.quote: If a Yezidi is forcibly dragged out of a circle, he immediately falls into the state called catalepsy.

stops.name: Kars: the family follows the fallen fortress
stops.campa: The guns of the Tsar have taken Kars, and ruin has taken the Giorgiades herds: a cattle plague eats the family fortune in a season. The father, proud and unbowed, moves the household to the newly Russian fortress town and opens a carpenter's shop. Kars is a garrison Babel: Cossacks, Greeks, Armenians, Tatars, Molokan sectarians, all pressed inside grey basalt walls under a citadel. Here the boy will be forged, between the workshop's poverty and the cathedral's chant.

stops.name: Kars, the military cathedral: Dean Borsh
stops.campa: His voice earns him a place in the choir of the fortress cathedral, and the choir brings him under the eye of Dean Borsh, master of the garrison's souls. The old priest, hearing the boy argue, takes him from the municipal school and teaches him alone: mathematics, astronomy, Latin, the making of a man. Borsh and the father sit evenings trading questions about God and the world while the boy listens from the shadows. The Dean's design is set: the boy shall be both physician of the body and confessor of the soul, for neither alone can heal a man.
stops.quote: The man who was soon to become my first tutor, the founder and creator of my present individuality, and, so to say, the 'third aspect of my inner God'.
stops.quote_source: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'My Father' (of Dean Borsh)

stops.name: Kars, Gilgamesh by the hearth
stops.campa: Winter nights, the father sings. He is an ashokh, a contest bard who has stood against the best singers of Van and Karabagh, and among his songs is the oldest of all: the tale of Gilgamesh, carried mouth to mouth for thousands of years. The boy hears of the Flood before the Flood and does not forget a line. Decades later he will read in a magazine that tablets dug from the ruins of Nineveh carry the very verses his father sang by the hearth, proof that a song can outlast empires, passed unwritten across five thousand years, and he will weep at the confirmation.
stops.quote: I will tell thee, Gilgamesh, / Of a mournful mystery of the Gods: / How once, having met together, / They resolved to flood the land of Shuruppak.
stops.quote_source: The father's recitation as recorded in Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'My Father'

stops.name: The saint's tomb beyond Alexandropol: the paralytic walks and the rain falls
stops.campa: Wonders multiply and refuse the schoolbooks. A paralytic who cannot lift a spoon has himself dragged on a cart to the tomb of a saint on the hill; he kisses the stone, and before the day is out he walks back down on his own legs. In a rainless summer the whole town, Orthodox, Armenian, Muslim alike, follows the archimandrite and the icon into the parched fields; before the procession regains the gates the sky breaks open and drenches them. The boy stands in the miracle rain, counting what his physics cannot count.

stops.name: Alexandropol, the table that raps
stops.campa: At his aunt's house a three-legged table answers questions, knocking out letters and numbers for the dead. A fortune-teller traces his palm and reads a wound that has not yet happened: a gun, a right side, a far country; years later the stray bullets will keep her appointment. He devours books of neurology and hypnotism, interrogates priests and doctors, and finds every explanation thinner than the facts. The choice hardens in him: he will not rest until he knows the meaning and purpose of life on earth, whatever it costs and wherever the answer hides.

stops.name: Tiflis, the stoker who reads Greek
stops.campa: Too restless for the seminary road laid out for him, he goes to Tiflis and shovels coal for the Transcaucasian Railway, sleeping among firemen and reading by lamp. In the city of sulphur baths and caravanserais he finds his first brothers of the search: Sarkis Pogossian, a theological student who cannot sit still, and soon Abram Yelov, the bookstall Assyrian who can find any volume in any tongue. They pool their books and their questions. The Seekers of Truth begin here, in soot and argument, before they have a name.

stops.name: Echmiadzin, the holy see that does not answer
stops.campa: With Pogossian he walks as a pilgrim to Echmiadzin, the Vatican of Armenia, where the chrism of a whole people is boiled in a cauldron once every seven years. They lodge weeks in the hostel for pilgrims, question monks, stand through the long chants under Ararat's white witness. The liturgy is magnificent and the answer is not there. He leaves with the certainty that what he seeks was known once and has been withdrawn from the open churches, driven underground, into ruins and brotherhoods. The search turns from the altar toward the buried.

stops.name: Ani, the parchments in the ruined city
stops.campa: In the dead capital of a thousand and one churches, he and Pogossian camp among the ruins and dig. Under a collapsed passage of a monastery they break into a monk's cell and find letters on parchment, monk to monk, in old Armenian. One line stops their breath: word of the Sarmoung Brotherhood, a famous esoteric school, and of where its heirs had gone. A word he has already met in the old book Merkhavat now stands in his hands with an address attached: somewhere between Urmia and Kurdistan. The digging stops; the journey begins.
stops.quote: This word is the name of a famous esoteric school which, according to tradition, was founded in Babylon.

stops.name: The road through Turkish Armenia, the map of pre-sand Egypt
stops.campa: Traveling disguised toward Mesopotamia on the trail of the Sarmoung, they shelter in the house of an Armenian priest. Among the old man's relics is a parchment map that will not let Gurdjieff sleep: Egypt drawn before the sands: the Sphinx and the great works standing in a country that has not yet been buried. He trembles as over treasure; the priest will not sell, so through a night he copies it secretly, line by line, and afterward carries the copy against his chest through bazaars and frontiers, oilcloth-wrapped, like a second heart.
